name: Christian Conservatism
summary: A politics that applies traditional Christian moral teaching to public life, chiefly in the United States through the Christian right. It defends the sanctity of life from conception, marriage as the union of one man and one woman, distinct male and female roles, religious liberty and a larger public role for religion, and it usually allies these with capitalism, lower taxes, strong defence and national sovereignty.
scope: The mainstream conservative Protestant (evangelical) and traditionalist Catholic politics of the American Christian right, as set out in the Manhattan Declaration (2009) and Nashville Statement (2017) and documented in scholarship on the Christian right. It excludes the theological category of conservative Christianity as such, Christian democracy, and theonomic Reconstructionism; economic and foreign-policy answers reflect the Republican-aligned majority, and Catholic social teaching dissent is noted where it matters.

keyFigures.name: Paul Weyrich
keyFigures.role: Conservative activist who helped organise the Christian right and framed the IRS dispute over religious schools as a religious-freedom issue.

sources.title: Christian right
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Policy positions on school prayer, creationism, vouchers, pornography, economics, death penalty, Israel, Christian nationalism, and internal disagreements.

sources.title: The Manhattan Declaration: A Call of Christian Conscience
sources.author: Orthodox, Catholic and Evangelical signatories
sources.usedFor: Life, marriage, religious liberty, civil disobedience, concern for the poor and rule of law.

sources.title: The Nashville Statement
sources.author: Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood
sources.usedFor: Sexuality outside marriage, distinct male and female design, transgender identity and the post-Christian culture.

sources.title: Conservative Christianity
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Theological commitments: biblical authority, creeds, complementarianism, and the distinction from political conservatism.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Adherents mostly favour private and charitable provision and opposition to state expansion, though the Manhattan Declaration stresses care for the vulnerable; the stance is a loose fit, so this is a low-confidence lean.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The Christian right grew alongside supply-side conservatism and opposed the Great Society, which suggests scepticism toward wage mandates, but no source addresses wage floors directly.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: White evangelicals rank among the strongest supporters of capitalism as central to American identity, and Reagan-era leaders paired social conservatism with deregulation.

public-ownership.rationale: The Christian right backed tax cuts, deregulation and opposed the New Deal, so nationalising industry runs against its economic outlook.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Christian right groups back tax cuts and child tax credits rather than higher taxes on the rich.

unions-good.rationale: Early fundamentalists and Reagan-era leaders were generally hostile to organised labour, though Catholic members accept the Church's support for unions, so the answer leans negative with low confidence.

property-fundamental.rationale: Early American fundamentalists favoured laissez-faire and property protection, and the movement defends it as a conservative principle, though no source states property as a right.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The movement combined social conservatism with deregulation under Reagan and does not push tighter corporate regulation.

cut-welfare.rationale: The Christian right opposed the Great Society, yet the Manhattan Declaration shows special concern for the poor and some adherents favour aid; the movement has no unified line on this.

worker-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the sources proposes worker ownership; capitalist commitments of the movement point to disagreement, but the issue is peripheral.

surveillance-ok.rationale: The movement gives national security and civil liberty both weight and the sources say little; no single position stands out.

legalize-drugs.rationale: The Christian right opposes drug use, historically supporting temperance, so legalising recreational drugs is rejected.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration warns that hate-crime and anti-discrimination laws threaten religious expression, so adherents distrust speech restrictions.

strong-leader.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms the rule of law and obedience only to just authority; some adherents have backed strong leaders like Trump, but the principled stance is against bypassing law.

state-harmful.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms law and government as serving justice and the common good, so anarchist views are rejected.

limit-guns.rationale: American social conservatism groups doctrinal Christian conservatives alongside gun-rights conservatives, so strict limits are opposed by most adherents.

empower-police-military.rationale: Law-and-order and a strong defence posture are standard in the Reagan-era coalition the Christian right belonged to.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Sexual intimacy is reserved for marriage in the Nashville Statement, so commercial sex is rejected morally and adherents oppose legalising it.

decide-locally.rationale: Christian right activists use both local control (schools, states) and national action (Roe, marriage amendments); sources give no single line.

rehabilitation.rationale: Evangelical prison ministries stress redemption while the movement also favours harsher punishment, so adherents lean both ways.

traditional-family.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration calls marriage the foundation of society and urges rebuilding a marriage culture around the conjugal union of man and woman.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration defines marriage as the union of man and woman and opposes redefining it; the Nashville Statement denies marriage can be same-sex.

abortion-legal.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration opposes abortion and affirms the sanctity of life from conception; the Christian right sought to overturn Roe v. Wade.

more-religion-public.rationale: The Christian right supports school prayer, Ten Commandments displays and funding for religious schools and charities.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The movement mainly frames civil rights through religious liberty and colour-blind terms; the Manhattan Declaration praises King, but active policy correction is not a stated aim.

gender-social-construct.rationale: The Nashville Statement says men and women are distinct by design and that biological sex grounds identity, rejecting construction.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Christian nationalism and patriotic defence of the nation's Christian heritage are widespread in the movement.

gradual-change.rationale: As a conservative movement defending creed and tradition it favours continuity of institutions over rapid change, though that is a general trait.

reduce-immigration.rationale: White evangelicals are unmatched in pessimism about border migration, with 70 percent calling it a crisis, though they back some path to legal status.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Sovereignty-minded conservatism distrusts the UN; the sources say little on it directly.

free-trade.rationale: Free-trade traditions conflict with growing support for tariffs among white evangelicals, with about two thirds backing Trump's tariffs in 2025.

nation-first.rationale: Christian nationalism and the tariff turn show a pro-national stance, though not a rejection of cooperation.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Hawkish and non-interventionist evangelicals both exist; sources only note Christian Zionist foreign policy.

open-borders.rationale: A majority of evangelicals call border migration a crisis, and the movement favours defined borders and national culture.

limit-growth.rationale: The movement strongly supports capitalism and growth; the Cornwall Declaration-type stance sees growth as aiding stewardship, so limiting it is rejected.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Evangelical conservatives broadly support deregulation and oppose mandatory emissions cuts as costly, but a minority of younger evangelicals disagree.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: No source takes a position; Christian doctrine stresses sin and grace as the human problem, tempering technological optimism.

expand-nuclear.rationale: No source addresses it; it follows from the pro-energy, pro-growth economics of the movement.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms obedience to law except where gravely unjust and then only conscientious disobedience, not revolution.

experts-over-public.rationale: The movement is hostile to academic and media elites on cultural issues, though it values expert theologians; the answer is a lean only.

central-planning.rationale: The movement opposed the New Deal and backs capitalism strongly.

socialized-markets.rationale: Support for capitalism makes public or worker-owned markets unattractive but adherents are not hostile to cooperatives in principle.

land-value-tax.rationale: No source addresses it; a single tax replacing others is a niche idea that tax-cut-oriented conservatives rarely adopt.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Christian right groups back tax cuts and family-oriented tax relief, which includes opposing death taxes.

basic-income.rationale: No source addresses it; unconditional payments conflict with the work ethic emphasised by many adherents.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: About two thirds of white evangelicals backed Trump's tariffs in 2025, but free-trade traditions persist among adherents.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The movement's capitalist leanings and opposition to the New Deal imply scepticism of state-directed industry.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Sources do not document it; Catholic distributist voices exist but mainstream American evangelicals do not push it.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Strong support for capitalism and private economy excludes abolishing money.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Not a stated plank of Christian conservatism, though libertarian-leaning members hold it.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Catholic social teaching supports corporatist ideas but the American movement favours free bargaining and deregulation.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms rule of law and conscience and the movement works through competitive elections.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Christian conservatism does not require monarchy; sources are silent and views differ by country.

democracy-best.rationale: The movement works in democratic politics and the Manhattan Declaration speaks of citizens' duty, though it holds moral limits on what voters may choose.

direct-votes.rationale: Referendums were used for marriage amendments, but principled preference for direct democracy is not documented.

workers-councils.rationale: Council communism contradicts the capitalism and constitutional order the movement defends.

right-to-secede.rationale: The sources do not discuss it; the movement's patriotism leans against secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration stresses equal dignity of every person, which tells against a doctrine of natural rulers.

political-violence-never.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration praises King's nonviolent disobedience, but many adherents accept just-war or defensive violence; positions vary.

war-builds-character.rationale: No source states it; Christian ethics do not prize war.

separate-church-state.rationale: Christian nationalists argue the Constitution does not require separation and Alliance Defending Freedom treats separation as a tool against Christians.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Supporters push Ten Commandments displays and biblical influence in law, though mainstream adherents stop short of full scriptural law.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration sees law and order as government's duty to protect the weak.

military-superiority.rationale: Reagan-era Christian right was hawkish on defence and strongly pro-military.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms the dignity of every person, and mainstream Christian conservatism defines the nation by culture and faith, not ethnicity.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Conservative Christianity grounds history in providence and creeds, not materialist class conflict.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The movement backs capitalism and opposed the Great Society, rejecting equal outcomes.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: No source addresses it; views differ among adherents.

colonial-reparations.rationale: The movement is hostile to reparations-style programs and prizes national tradition.

civilizational-union.rationale: Sources do not discuss it; some adherents favour a Christian-West identity but not political union.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Christian teaching puts love of neighbour over self-interest, although the movement supports markets.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration stresses duties and conscience rights alike, and no source ranks them.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Conservative Christianity treats nature as God's creation under human stewardship rather than as having value apart from humans.

limit-population.rationale: The movement opposes abortion and promotes large families, and dismisses overpopulation fears.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Strong pro-capitalism and pro-growth stance rejects the claim.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration opposes embryo-destructive research and cloning, signalling caution about disruptive technology.

human-enhancement.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration opposes cloning and embryo-destructive research on grounds of human dignity.

algorithmic-government.rationale: No source addresses it; moral responsibility of rulers is central to the declaration.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Sources do not address it; both civil-libertarian and security views occur.

restore-past-order.rationale: The Nashville Statement frames accommodation to a post-Christian culture as a failing, favouring return to historic norms, though restoration is not set against all progress.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Conservative Christianity grounds policy in doctrine and moral principle rather than purely results.

direct-action.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration endorses lawful witness and conscientious disobedience but works through elections and courts.

means-match-ends.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration insists on love and respect in pursuing its goals, but this is a general principle only.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Rejected by a capitalist, market-oriented movement.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Material needs are a Christian concern, but the movement rejects distribution by state according to need over work.

production-for-use.rationale: Capitalism's profit motive is endorsed by most adherents.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The movement strongly supports capitalism and does not see profit as exploitation.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Contradicts rule of law and religious liberty.

collective-farming.rationale: Collectivisation contradicts the movement's property and market commitments.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The movement champions capitalism and rejects Marxist theory of imperialism.

taxation-theft.rationale: The movement favours lower taxes yet the Manhattan Declaration affirms government's legitimate role, so it rejects the strong claim.

harm-principle.rationale: The Nashville Statement and Manhattan Declaration defend morals law beyond preventing harm (marriage, pornography, drugs).

individual-rights-only.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration claims religious liberty for institutions and families as well as individuals.

conscription.rationale: Patriotic, pro-military adherents accept the draft in principle while libertarian-leaning members resist it; the sources record no stance.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The movement values political participation and voting, though emigration is not discussed.

state-as-business.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration gives government a moral purpose of justice and protecting the weak, which sits poorly with treating citizens as customers; the sources do not address it directly.

positive-liberty.rationale: The movement is sceptical of expanded welfare-state rights, favouring negative liberty and religious freedom.

media-academia-power.rationale: The Christian right treats universities and media as hostile cultural powers, and the Nashville Statement describes a post-Christian culture.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms equal dignity of all, and mainstream adherents reject racial hierarchy.

organic-representation.rationale: The movement operates through parties and lobbying groups like Focus on the Family.

total-state.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration holds conscience belongs to God alone, limiting the state.

national-rebirth.rationale: Calls to restore a Christian culture from decadence appear in the Nashville Statement's preamble and in Christian nationalism.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Not a stated aim; the movement's foreign policy is mainly defensive and pro-Israel.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Rule of law is affirmed in the Manhattan Declaration.

bound-labor.rationale: Rejected by the equal dignity of all and the Declaration's concern for the vulnerable.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Conservative Christianity claims objective truth in scripture and creed.

universal-morality.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration appeals to moral truths and natural law binding all, grounding its claims on life and marriage in universal reasons as well as scripture.

single-common-good.rationale: The Declaration says law exists to preserve order and serve justice and the common good, treating politics as aimed at a shared good.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Many evangelical supporters strongly back Christian Zionism and Israel, with 80 percent in a 2017 poll holding the prophetic belief, though some churches reject its religious basis.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: A question of ethnic-national politics; Christian Zionist support for Israel's immigration law hints at sympathy, but the sources record no general stance.

revive-national-language.rationale: Not a concern of the movement; no source addresses it.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The movement backs deregulation and capitalism, rejecting mandated worker voice.

school-vouchers.rationale: The Christian right increasingly supports school vouchers and public funding for religious schools.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Reagan-era fiscal conservatism shaped the Christian right and tax cuts rather than stimulus are its preference.

economic-freedom.rationale: White evangelicals are among the strongest backers of capitalism as central to American identity.

rule-by-example.rationale: Christian ethics honour rulers' moral example, yet the Manhattan Declaration relies on law and the rule of law to preserve order, so adherents would not choose either pole.

national-self-determination.rationale: Patriotic and nationalist outlook favours national sovereignty, though the issue is peripheral.

force-without-un.rationale: The Reagan-era hawkish stance favours sovereign decision on force, without need for UN approval.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Conservative Christianity holds biblical authority and creeds over secular reason as the final guide.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Evangelical pessimism on immigration and nation-first views support reserving benefits for citizens.

work-for-welfare.rationale: The Christian right opposed the Great Society and favours work requirements consistent with the work ethic.

class-collaboration.rationale: Capitalist cooperation between employers and workers fits the movement, and it rejects class struggle.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Conservative Christianity defends inherited creeds and traditions of the church and culture.

dominated-front.rationale: A third-world anti-Western front is alien to a movement that sees itself as part of the West, and the sources never discuss it.

workers-nation.rationale: Class-based organisation of any kind is outside the movement, whose coalition is defined by faith and morals rather than class or nation of workers.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Nashville Statement says men and women are equal in dignity but distinct by design, and Focus on the Family emphasises gender roles, but law-level role distinctions are less clearly demanded.

ban-interest.rationale: The movement champions capitalism, so banning interest is rejected.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration praises King's Letter from Birmingham Jail and affirms equal dignity.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Marxist view of the state is rejected by the movement.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Evangelical conservative groups have opposed mandatory emissions cuts and favoured cheap energy, aligning with expanded oil, gas and coal.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Concern with national Christian culture leads adherents to expect assimilation, and white evangelicals see immigrants as threat to customs.

elite-replacement.rationale: Mainstream Christian right leaders do not endorse the replacement claim, though some adherents echo it online; the sources record no stance.

proportional-representation.rationale: The movement works within US plurality voting; not documented.

national-mission.rationale: Christian nationalism holds America has a Christian founding and mission, but not necessarily of spreading its government.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The Nashville Statement holds male-female distinctions are good by design, not a systemic injustice.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Christian right shares populist distrust of political elites, and some factions backed Trump against them.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration defends the unborn, disabled and elderly against threat to their lives, and opposes eugenic practices.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: A law-and-order movement is wary of prosecuting past security-force actions, yet the Declaration upholds protection for the vulnerable; no source settles it.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The movement wants government to enforce morals and protect the vulnerable beyond a night-watchman role.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms the equal dignity of all and does not endorse racial separation.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration calls for protecting every member of society, including the most marginalized and voiceless, and the Nashville Statement says men and women are equal in dignity and worth.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Marxist doctrinal matter the movement does not address.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The Christian right is patriotic and rejects that framing of the US and Israel.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Christian conservatives want exemptions for religious conscience, which cuts against uniform law, but they also favour one national law on marriage; no stated position.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration says God alone is Lord of the conscience and defends religious liberty, though evangelists seek converts.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not a Christian concern, and it opposes such restriction as foreign to its tradition.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Christian right supports school prayer and putting the Bible and Ten Commandments into public school curricula.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Manhattan Declaration calls government a servant of justice and the common good, but also stresses authority from God.

trade-surplus.rationale: Economic nationalists among adherents favour surpluses and tariffs, while free-trade adherents do not; the sources report only the split over tariffs.

population-transfer.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration's equal dignity and concern for the vulnerable contradicts forced removal.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Christian conservatives accept just war and law enforcement, so absolute rejection of force fails.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Support for capitalism favours competition, but Christian ethics do not frame struggle between peoples as progress.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: The movement values constitutional order but also fears state power against dissent; no source addresses party bans.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: A republican-theory concept that the movement's sources do not use; its religious-liberty claims share some of the spirit, but nothing fixes a position.

separated-powers.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms the rule of law and constitutional order, and the movement criticises activist courts and distrusts concentrated power.

vanguard-party.rationale: Marxist doctrine rejected by the movement.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration expresses a special concern for the poor and vulnerable, though it does not make them first claim on law.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: A UK policy; the property-owning outlook of the Reagan-era right would favour it, but Christian conservative sources do not address council housing.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Reagan-era coalition curbed union power, but no source addresses it directly.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The movement rejects overpopulation arguments, defending life and large families.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Sources note concern about immigrants and national culture but adherents differ on diversity's effects.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Not a Christian conservative proposal; alien to the movement's electoral politics.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration stresses rule of law, but some adherents accept emergency powers.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The movement's free-market stance opposes price controls.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration defends religious liberty and conscience, rejecting state control of information.

party-commands-army.rationale: Rule of law and constitutional order contradict party command of the army.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Concern about immigration and national culture supports long waits, though many evangelicals back a path to status.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Not a concern of the Christian right, whose sources never address legislators' pay.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The movement works through lobbies and voters' consciences rather than disciplined parties; sources do not address party discipline.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Sovereignty-minded conservatism opposes pooling sovereignty in bodies like the EU.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Sources never discuss executive command arrangements; US-style presidential command is the default in the movement's own country.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Conservative Christianity spans episcopal, Presbyterian and congregational polities with no single answer.

clerical-rule.rationale: American Christian conservatives, including Southern Baptists, hold clergy are not to rule the state, and the Christian right works through lay politics.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: The patriotic movement supports its own country in war.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The movement opposes pornography but its attitude to censoring art is not documented, and free-speech instincts compete.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Constitutional limits are part of the order the movement defends, but it has no stated view on term limits for presidents.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall is a procedural device that the Christian right neither pushes nor opposes in its sources.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Hawkish pro-military and pro-Israel foreign policy favours alliances.

people-in-arms.rationale: Gun-rights conservatives hold a militia view, but replacing a professional army is not a stated aim.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Traditionalist culture often idealises small-town and rural life, but the sources do not state it as a doctrine.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: A matter of national politics outside the movement's documented concerns.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Christian right treats universities as hostile cultural institutions, aligning with populist critique.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Conservative Christianity holds Christian truth to be superior to other religions.

death-penalty.rationale: The Southern Baptist Convention and Missouri Synod Lutherans support it, and evangelicals are likelier than others to favour it, though Catholics oppose.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: The Christian right campaigned for abstinence-only sex education and opposes gender content.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The Christian right supports including creationism in public school textbooks and opposes teaching evolution.

restrict-pornography.rationale: The Christian right is documented as opposing pornography.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The movement's immigration caution suggests some sympathy, but the sources do not address birthright citizenship.

minority-language-support.rationale: Conservative language politics usually leans toward one national language, but Christian conservative sources are silent.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration defends conscience rights and the Alliance Defending Freedom seeks exemptions from anti-discrimination law.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Conservative Christianity values moral conformity to creed and tradition over eccentricity.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Christian debt relief appeals exist (Jubilee), but the American movement has not adopted them.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: A post-colonial socialist claim that the movement's capitalist outlook would not accept, though the sources never address it.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The movement defends the existing constitutional order, so a rewrite by assembly is not on its agenda; sources are silent.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The movement defends liberty of conscience and the rule of law.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration notes Christian work for the poor and clean water in developing nations as part of its moral concern, though governmental aid is not demanded.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Reagan-era strong-defence outlook favours independent deterrents.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: No source addresses how a head of state is chosen; in the US this is settled by the Electoral College which adherents accept.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Sources do not address monetary institutions; Christian conservatism has no doctrine on central banks.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Christian Zionist evangelicals strongly back Israel's claims; 80 percent in a 2017 poll held the prophetic belief.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Catholic members hold this via social teaching but evangelical members defend property more absolutely.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Not a Christian conservative issue; they condemn Soviet communism but not on this theory.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Evangelical conservatives have opposed precautionary regulation such as mandatory emissions cuts.

collective-defense.rationale: The hawkish Reagan-era coalition supported NATO-style defence.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The sources do not address annexation or occupation law; Christian Zionist adherents would deny the claim as applied to Israel while others would not.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration warns against regulations that burden religious institutions, such as charities, in the name of anti-discrimination.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The statement fits monarchies and parliamentary systems; the American movement treats the presidency as partisan, and sources record no stance.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The patriotic movement would likely resist breakup but sources do not discuss it.

region-keeps-system.rationale: A question about Hong Kong-style autonomy that the movement does not address.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Christian conservatism holds that God alone is Lord of the conscience, and denies divinity of rulers.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The Christian right backs tax cuts, and flat-tax proposals fit within its fiscal conservatism.

character-from-environment.rationale: The Nashville Statement and sin doctrine stress innate nature and moral agency over environment.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Declaration affirms rule of law and that unjust law may be disobeyed.

space-expansion.rationale: A technology-policy goal outside the movement's moral and cultural concerns.

mixed-constitution.rationale: A classical-republican theory; the sources do not discuss it though adherents revere the US founding's mixed institutions.

leader-cult.rationale: God alone is Lord, so idolising leaders contradicts doctrine, though some adherents have venerated political figures.

equal-parenting.rationale: Fathers' rights concerns exist in the movement, but the sources record no position on custody presumptions.

land-redistribution.rationale: Contradicts property commitments of the movement.

refugee-return.rationale: Christian Zionist support for Israel makes adherents cool to Palestinian return, but the sources do not state a position.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The movement defends sovereign borders and the sources never endorse claims on territory because co-nationals live there.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration holds God alone is Lord of the conscience; US Christian conservatives defend freedom to leave a religion.

women-must-cover.rationale: Contradicts religious liberty and the movement's practice; not a Christian conservative demand.

common-currency.rationale: Sovereignty-minded conservatism favours national currencies, though sources do not address it.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-national unions are foreign to the Christian right, whose sources do not discuss them.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: A Central European minority-rights doctrine that the American movement's sources do not engage.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: A Jewish diaspora debate that Christian conservative sources do not engage, though Christian Zionist support for Israel suggests sympathy for a homeland.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Conservative Christianity grounds history in providence, ideas and morality.

ban-cartels.rationale: Free-market conservatism opposes regulation but not monopolies as such; the sources do not discuss antitrust.

no-bailouts.rationale: Free-market conservatism and Reagan-era politics oppose bailouts, though not a distinct plank.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration speaks of courts and law but adherents also criticise judicial activism and favour majority will on moral issues; mixed.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Distinct gender roles in the Nashville Statement and conservative stance oppose quotas.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Tariff support is growing among adherents, but autarkic imperial blocs are never proposed in the sources.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Free-market conservatism opposes mandated standards, and some oppose to protect cheap energy.

moral-incentives.rationale: The movement is pro-market and material incentives.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The movement favours law and conscience, rejecting revolutionary violence.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Titles are not a concern in the American movement, whose sources do not address them.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Christian nationalists and the movement want history taught with a Christian founding and national centre.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Missionary heritage gives some adherents sympathy, but modern Christian conservative sources do not defend tutelage.

patriotic-education.rationale: Christian nationalism and the push to put Bible and Ten Commandments in schools implies pride in nation's heritage.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: The movement is generally aligned with conservative opposition to racial preferences, though the sources do not document it directly.

public-money-creation.rationale: Monetary reform is outside the movement's documented concerns, and its market outlook leans against it.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: The movement's strong capitalism support implies belief it survives crises.

former-empire-influence.rationale: A foreign-policy question about post-imperial spheres that the sources do not address.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration seeks religious exemptions from anti-discrimination law but does not defend discrimination on all grounds.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration defends constitutionally guaranteed religious liberty and conscience.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: No Christian conservative source discusses colonial treaties.

elective-rulers.rationale: The movement works in an elective democracy, but the sources do not address monarchy versus election.

minority-veto.rationale: Liberum veto is an obscure principle never discussed in the sources, and the movement works by majority and court rule.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration cites Acts 4 and says unjust laws need not be obeyed, but it does not endorse removal of rulers.

parliament-supreme.rationale: A statement about Westminster monarchy; American adherents treat the Constitution, not the legislature, as supreme.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Christian stewardship teaches kindness to animals, though human dignity ranks above.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Stewardship allows use of animals under limits on cruelty.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration stresses a special concern for the vulnerable and notes historical Christian service to poor and orphans.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration calls Christians to engage in public life and defend life, marriage and liberty.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The Nashville Statement criticises post-Christian culture, though it does not frame this as pacification.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: A Gramscian theory the sources do not discuss.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency theory contradicts the pro-capitalist outlook.

native-born-offices.rationale: The movement's nation-first views suggest sympathy, but no source states a rule limiting offices to native-born citizens.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Foreign-aid views vary: fiscal conservatives resist aid while evangelical missions give relief; no source states a position.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentism is not part of the movement's documented concerns.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: A question the movement's sources never address, and its equal-dignity stance cuts against group-based leadership.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Sources do not address constitutional founding values of this kind.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Reagan-era anti-communism condemned totalitarianism, and the Manhattan Declaration defends conscience against tyranny.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Historical debate not addressed in the sources; adherents are found on both sides.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Christian nationalism and patriotic heritage favour keeping monuments, as a general conservative position.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The movement stresses fathers and men's roles, but the sources do not address programmes for boys and men.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The sources record no position on domestic-violence services.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Christian universalism pulls against civilizational relativism, while Christian nationalism pulls the other way; sources record no stance.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The Declaration affirms civilian rule of law, and the movement works through elections.

paid-care-work.rationale: Distinct family roles and pro-family tax relief favour support for the family, not wages for housework.

filial-duty.rationale: The movement upholds the family; the Ten Commandments honour parents, which the Christian right promotes in public life.

office-by-exam.rationale: The Confucian civil-service principle is not part of Christian conservative thought.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Tariff nationalists favour it and free-market adherents oppose it; the sources do not say.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration calls for reconsidering unilateral divorce as part of rebuilding a marriage culture.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Imperative mandate is a left-democratic idea, and the movement works through ordinary representation.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Market-minded conservatives favour private accounts, but the sources do not address pensions.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The Declaration affirms the rule of law and constitutional order.

single-official-language.rationale: Christian conservatives in the US often back English as official language, but the sources never take up language policy.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Nation-first views might support limits, but the sources do not address foreign land ownership.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: The Christian right favours colour-blind law and opposes race-conscious remedies, so outcome-based discrimination tests are rejected.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Christian teaching warns against materialism, and many adherents agree, even as the movement defends capitalism.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: The Reagan-era coalition backed anti-communist insurgents, but the Christian right has no settled doctrine on arming insurgents today.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Cold War hawkishness tolerated bloc interventions, yet a religious-liberty movement has no stated view on this specific doctrine.

corporate-influence.rationale: Populists in the movement criticise big business while the pro-capitalist majority defends it, so no clear stance.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: No source addresses foreign funding rules; sovereignty-minded adherents may favour it while religious groups rely on overseas partners.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Christian right groups back child tax credits and pro-family tax policy, and the movement celebrates large families over population control.

residents-only-property.rationale: Property-rights commitments cut against local purchase limits, though the sources do not discuss them.

job-guarantee.rationale: The Christian right opposed the Great Society and backs a market economy, so a government job guarantee runs against it.

democratic-peace.rationale: The sources never address democratic peace theory; Reagan-era conservatives valued democracy promotion but the Christian right as such has no stated view.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms a duty to obey law unless it is gravely unjust, so a general duty is held with exceptions.

non-intervention.rationale: Hawkish pro-military views and Christian Zionist support for Israel favour some intervention abroad.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union organisation form is not a Christian conservative concern in the sources.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration affirms the dignity of all, and mainstream leaders reject conspiracy theories about minorities, though fringes exist.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration calls for rebuilding a marriage culture and defines marriage legally as the conjugal union of man and woman.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Sources do not discuss transparency; no distinctive Christian conservative position follows.

local-production.rationale: Not a stated concern; localist voices like Rod Dreher exist but they are not the mainstream.

informal-organisation.rationale: The movement builds permanent institutions such as churches, lobbies and legal groups, not informal affinity groups.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Sovereignty-minded conservatism prefers national courts over international ones, and the movement distrusts the UN.

religious-nation.rationale: Christian nationalists define America by Christian faith but other adherents reject faith-based citizenship.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Not a stated aim and the patriotic movement rejects tributary deference.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Not a stated aim; the sources do not discuss fiscal federalism.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Defence of private property by the movement covers personal belongings, but the clause about common ownership of production is rejected, so the statement is mixed.

defeat-communism.rationale: Reagan-era anti-communism was central to the Christian right coalition.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: School vouchers and funding for religious charities show openness to mixed provision, though health systems are not addressed.

religion-illusion.rationale: Conservative Christianity holds the historic creeds and the truth of Christian doctrine, rejecting the claim that religion is illusion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: White evangelicals are among the strongest supporters of capitalism as central to American identity.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Nashville Statement locates women's flourishing in distinct roles by design, not economic transformation.

socialized-care.rationale: The movement stresses the family, with distinct gender roles, as the place for childcare and housework.

purge-loanwords.rationale: No source addresses language purism, and nothing in Christian conservatism requires it.

treaties-binding.rationale: The sources do not address Indigenous treaties.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Intentional communities exist among Christians but the mainstream movement does not advocate reorganising society that way.

majority-settlement.rationale: Contradicts the Manhattan Declaration's equal dignity and justice for all.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The American Christian right firmly sides with capitalism, though Catholic social teaching proposes a third way.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Christian Zionism rests on biblical and historical claims to the land of Israel.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Mainstream Christian conservative leaders reject denial and the Manhattan Declaration affirms dignity of all.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration says rejection of sin must never become rejection of sinners, and it defends marriage law rather than criminal penalties.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration defends conscience and rule of law.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Most US Christian conservatives defend religious liberty and do not advocate punishing blasphemy, though Reconstructionists do.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Not a stated position and it conflicts with the Declaration's concern for justice.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Islamic concept outside Christian conservatism, which does not claim such duty.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The Declaration says to obey authority except where laws are gravely unjust, not to remove non-religious rulers by force.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The movement mobilises citizens through churches yet works within representative structures, and the sources do not call for direct participation in workplaces.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The Nashville Statement rejects the framework and argues against reading identity in terms of oppression.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The Nashville Statement denies that transgender self-conception fits God's purposes.

assisted-dying.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration opposes assisted suicide and euthanasia as a threat to the vulnerable.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The Christian right is firmly aligned with the right and sees the divide as meaningful.

alienated-labor.rationale: Marxist concept; the movement defends capitalist work, though Catholic teaching values dignity of work.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Some adherents hold this strongly while others reject it; sources do not document a consensus.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration says God alone is Lord of the conscience and calls authority to serve God's justice, and many Christian nationalists hold that rulers answer to God.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Defence of religious liberty and exemptions implies opposing bans on religious dress.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: The sources record no position on harassment settlement rules.

social-market-economy.rationale: Catholic members accept social protection, while evangelicals favour laissez-faire, so no common view.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The Christian right is strongly pro-military.

rich-first.rationale: A Chinese reform doctrine that the Christian right's sources never engage.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Reagan-era Christian right favoured alliances and anti-communist alignment.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Not a concern of the movement, and its sources are silent on hereditary leadership.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Fiscal conservatism favours austerity, though the sources do not discuss the IMF.

property-franchise.rationale: The Declaration's equal dignity contradicts property qualifications.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Ecofeminist claim contradicted by the Nashville Statement's order of male and female and a stewardship view of nature.

reification.rationale: Marxist concept the movement does not address.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The movement defends capitalist press and sees media as left-leaning, not owned by the rich for them.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration professes belief in law and the rule of law.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration praises King and affirms equal dignity for every person.

online-participation.rationale: Not a topic in the movement's sources.

open-government-data.rationale: The sources record no position on transparency.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration defends liberty of conscience; US Christian conservatives do not seek legal bars to interfaith marriage.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Contradicts the Declaration's dignity of all.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Sortition panels are not part of the movement's agenda, which relies on elected bodies and courts.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Conservative Christianity retains traditional creeds and rejects reinterpreting doctrine to modern conditions, as in the 2002 Anglican walkout.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Capitalist movement does not see wealth concentration as a threat to liberty.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: The Christian right opposes gay-rights measures and has resisted such policy changes.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The Christian right wants more religion in public life, so state promotion of atheism is rejected.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Law-and-order stance of the movement rejects abolition.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The sources do not address consociational arrangements.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration highlights Christian charity and the Christian right funds religious charities, though it does not reject all state aid.

term-limits.rationale: The sources record no position on legislative term limits.

vote-delegation.rationale: Liquid democracy is not a topic in the movement's sources.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Sources do not address it; Christian eschatology gives adherents a different frame for the end of the world.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Conservative Christianity's complementarianism restricts ordained leadership to men.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Complementarianism affirms male headship in the home, though many present it as loving leadership.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Nation-first and immigration-sceptical views oppose foreign voting.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Church youth groups exist but drilled national-service movements are not part of the Christian right's documented agenda.

recognise-genocide.rationale: The sources do not address recognition of genocides.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Capitalist returns to ownership are accepted, though work ethic is prized.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The movement is pro-gun and supports self-defence, and does not hold pacifism.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Christian nationalism stresses continuity of the nation's Christian founding, though the claim here is about ancient origins.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: The Nashville Statement ties biological sex to identity and denies it is a mere construct.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Contradicts the Nashville Statement's fixed male-female distinction.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Christian tradition honours martyrs, though for the faith, not the nation as stated.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The Nashville Statement frames cultural conflict as a choice between faithfulness and accommodation, and Christian nationalism uses spiritual warfare language.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: A Zionist debate that Christian conservative sources do not engage.

culture-before-state.rationale: The movement does stress cultural and moral renewal, but its sources do not rank it against state building.

god-not-male.rationale: Conservative Christianity retains traditional male language for God as in the creeds.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Conservative Christianity holds biblical authority over, not subject to, judgement.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Contradicts the movement's market principles and dignity of all.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: A territorial-politics question that the movement does not address.

independent-unions.rationale: The movement is cool to unions, and no source addresses their independence from parties.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Sources do not discuss local utilities, and the movement's market lean pulls against public ownership while local control favours it.

second-chamber.rationale: US constitutional order, which the movement defends, has a bicameral legislature.

confederal-coordination.rationale: A municipalist doctrine foreign to the movement.

family-wage.rationale: Pro-family economic stance and Catholic teaching favour a family wage, and the movement backs child tax credits.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Free-market adherents would favour it, while its bioethics concerns with embryo research are separate; sources are silent.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration opposes embryo research but sources do not address ageing research.

anonymous-payments.rationale: The sources record no position on payment privacy.

online-anonymity.rationale: The sources record no position on online anonymity.

person-over-state.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration holds every person has dignity and conscience that the state may not override.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Conservative Christianity affirms the human soul and body and spiritual goods, grounding the religious public role the movement seeks.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: The movement's federalist leanings and states' rights language give no clear answer in its sources.

gm-crops.rationale: Not a topic in the movement's sources.

dense-cities.rationale: The movement's family orientation and rural idealisation lean against, but sources do not address urban density.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The Declaration affirms equal dignity for all and does not rely on racial groups.

racial-pride.rationale: The sources record no position on racial pride, and adherents differ on it.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Hawkish foreign policy accepts preventive force and unilateral action.

language-defines-nation.rationale: The sources do not discuss language-based nationhood; the American movement defines the nation by creed and heritage.

communal-electorates.rationale: US Christian conservatives reject separate electorates by religion, and the movement works within common elections.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The sources record no such claim.

free-public-college.rationale: The movement opposes expanded entitlements and backs school choice, not free college.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Evangelical conservatives oppose mandatory emissions cuts and favour market-based or no regulation.

future-generations.rationale: Stewardship doctrine holds that humans must care for creation, though the movement stresses dignity over environmental limits.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The Nashville Statement says men and women are distinct by design, but political weight on women's values is not stated.

arms-reduction.rationale: Reagan-era peace through strength opposed unilateral reduction.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Sources do not address diplomatic secrecy.

capital-controls.rationale: Contradicts the market commitments of the movement.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Gun-rights conservatives defend private arms ownership.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The patriotic, pro-military movement rejects refusal.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The movement is cool to unions, though Catholic members accept them.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Contemporary Christian right groups back child tax credits and low-tax pro-work policy.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The movement favours existing free-market order.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Market-minded adherents favour economic freedom but no source endorses communities choosing different systems.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Sources do not discuss ecosystem valuation, and stewardship doctrine is expressed in religious terms.

sacred-nation.rationale: Christian nationalists treat the nation as divinely founded, but orthodox doctrine makes only God sacred.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Not a framing the movement adopts; contradicts its patriotic unity.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The Nashville Statement says male and female are given by design and rejects redefining human nature.

public-service-media.rationale: The Christian right distrusts mainstream media and favours less public funding.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Conservative Christianity holds historic creeds claim Christ as the unique truth.

farm-price-support.rationale: Rural conservatives often accept farm supports, while free-market adherents oppose them; sources are silent.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Reagan-era peace through strength favoured retaining deterrent.

workers-own-party.rationale: The movement works through the Republican coalition and rejects class parties.

ban-fgm.rationale: Defence of bodily integrity and dignity of the vulnerable implies support for a ban.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Nashville Statement affirms equal dignity and worth of women.

one-language-many-names.rationale: A linguistic-politics question that the movement's sources do not address.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: A libertarian environmental-law idea the sources do not address.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Not applicable to Western Christian conservatism and contradicts its constitutional politics.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Evangelical conservatives oppose emissions mandates as draconian, prizing liberty.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Law and order stance favours harsher fixed sentences.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Concern about national culture favours language requirements.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Reagan-era right-to-work conservatism is within the coalition, though the sources do not state it.

voter-id.rationale: Mainstream conservative policy position, adopted widely by Republican-aligned Christian right.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The Declaration unites Orthodox, Catholic and Evangelical but sources do not address legal status of doctrines.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration treats laws as bound by moral limits, but the procedural definition is not stated.

premarital-sex.rationale: The Nashville Statement reserves sexual intimacy for marriage.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: The Declaration defends conscience and speech; shutdowns conflict with that.

negative-income-tax.rationale: A Friedmanite welfare proposal the sources do not address.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Declaration affirms equal dignity and mainstream conservative Christians accept it.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: The Nashville Statement says men and women are equal in dignity and distinct by design, denying religion oppresses.

race-social-construct.rationale: Christian conservatives dispute race theory framing, but the sources do not discuss.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Distinct gender roles view opposes such agencies, which the movement sees as promoting gender ideology.

homestead-ownership.rationale: A Lockean property theory the sources do not discuss.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Conservative Christianity retains biblical authority, historical Genesis and creeds, and the movement treats scripture as inerrant.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Sources do not address Indigenous or national self-government arrangements.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Trotskyist doctrine opposed by the movement.

indirect-election.rationale: The sources do not address indirect election, though the movement defends the US Electoral College structure.

national-church-status.rationale: Evangelicals oppose established churches while Anglicans and Catholics favour one, so there is no common position.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The sources do not address territorial autonomy.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: The sources do not address referendums on territory.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: The sources do not address post-colonial borders.

simple-living.rationale: Christian ethics praise modest living but the movement defends prosperity and consumption; sources record no stance.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: The sources do not address indigenous-region migration policy.

equal-conscription.rationale: Distinct gender roles view favours men-only draft registration.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Christian Zionism and Christian nationalism stress bond to the holy land and the national homeland.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration stresses protecting life and the rule of law.

close-ties-china.rationale: The anti-communist, strong-defence coalition opposes closeness to China.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Concern for persecuted Christians abroad exists, but the sources do not discuss kin-state protection.

self-ownership.rationale: The Declaration sees persons as belonging to God, so self-ownership is not endorsed fully.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: The movement backs tax cuts generally, but the sources do not specify sales taxes.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The movement favours limited welfare, though not documented directly.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: The movement relies on lobbies and parties.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Pro-market adherents oppose cronyism, but populist adherents backed protections for chosen firms; no stated stance.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration unites Orthodox, Catholic and Evangelicals in cross-denominational politics, so the movement rejects limiting politics by denomination.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: The Nashville Statement and the movement favour modern society grounded in traditional creed.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Complementarian doctrine and the Manhattan Declaration's call to rethink unilateral divorce suggest scepticism, but the sources do not address women's right to initiate.

missingStatements.text: Citizens may refuse to obey a law that requires them to act against their conscience or religious faith.
missingStatements.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration cites Acts 4 and says its signers will not comply with edicts forcing participation in abortion or assisted suicide.

missingStatements.text: Research that destroys human embryos should be prohibited.
missingStatements.rationale: The Manhattan Declaration opposes embryo-destructive research and therapeutic cloning as threats to human life.
missingStatements.declined: Bioethics detail; abortion-legal and traditional-family already place the ideology.

missingStatements.text: Shops and public business should be restricted on one weekly day of rest.
missingStatements.rationale: The Christian right is documented as supporting Sunday Sabbatarianism and blue laws.
missingStatements.declined: Low-salience blue-law issue answered only +1; more-religion-public already places the ideology.

notes: Catholic and evangelical members diverge on the death penalty, unions, welfare and contraception; the answers follow the Republican-aligned majority. Support for tariffs and economic nationalism has grown since 2016. Many peripheral statements (constitutional design, territorial and monetary questions) are answered neutral or low because no source addresses them.
